newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Foncier bank sit-in nears end.
newsitem.headline: French Foncier bank sit-in nears end.

text.p: Staff protesters engaged in a sit-in at the Paris headquarters of French bank Credit Foncier look set to end a sit-in after several weeks on Thursday.
"The decision is probably already taken, but the staff will make their position known on Thursday at 9.30 am (0830 GMT)," a staff trade union official told Reuters.
"Nevertheless, the occupation continues tonight," Daniel Pellerin of the CFDT union added.

The union officials were speaking after a meeting in which Credit Foncier passed a largely technical resolution to bring its statutes in line with continued operations despite the hole in its books since reporting 1995 losses of 10.8 billion francs ($1.96 billion).
Several hundred staff occupied the downtown headquarters nearly three weeks ago in a battle to halt government plans for a partial takeover of the bank and a wind-down of the rest.
They held its chairman hostage for six days but the sit-in has now been toned down in terms of numbers and offices are open for business.

Staff are fighting a plan unveiled by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis in July, which would involve spinning off Foncier's property loans business to cooperatively run Credit Immobilier and shunting the rest into a state holding company to be shut down over time.

Le Monde newspaper said a report by Paribas bank had confirmed the possibility of Foncier making a profit of more than one billion francs ($170 million) this year but said that it could need a recapitalisation of up to six billion francs.

Arthuis has already carried out the first stage of his plan by getting the state-owned bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations to "nationalise" Foncier through a buyout of shareholders for more than two billion francs.
Credit Foncier was private but had top management named by the state because of its status as a "specialised financial institution" providing low-cost home loans to France's poorer families.
Unions argue the losses were overstated to fell the group and that it could still be made viable despite misadventures in property in the past.

Under Credit Foncier's statutes, which are different from those of ordinary companies, the 145-year-old bank should have plugged its balance sheet within four months and has stayed in business only following the state-sponsored takeover.
